extracted.intended_audience: reviewers for ACL Rolling Review (ARR) / NLP peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_short: ARR peer review for NLP papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing peer review on ARR (ACL Rolling Review) submissions in NLP, including assignment checks, writing reviews, scoring, discussion, and ethics/AI policies. Targets reviewers evaluating conference-style NLP papers (models, resources, analyses, theory, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All information about submissions and reviews received as part of an assignment is confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not identify individual submissions in public discussion or social media; ensure comments/examples are general enough that no submission can be identified. Do not submit confidential information to third-party services that may retain/use it (this includes some generative AI services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author anonymity and searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not actively try to discover the identity of the authors and should avoid letting any suspicion or knowledge of identity affect judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workflow: (1) read paper and form first impression, (2) search for related work only after that read and not deliberately to find that submission. If you uncover or believe you can identify authors, inform the area chair (not other reviewers) and disclose in the ARR form; consider asking for reassignment if COI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate time for reviewing and discussion (Task 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Block time in your calendar for checking assignments, working on reviews, and submitting them on time, and for the discussion/response period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate time per paper (skimming + in-depth reading, writing/editing ~half page). Spread work across days to avoid knee-jerk reactions. Clock yourself periodically to plan workload. Late reviews create extra work and harm authors' chance to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and conflict-of-interest (COI) check (Assignment check)
rubrics_metrics.description: On assignment, skim the paper to check whether you are qualified to review it and whether you have any COI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If expertise is partial, state in the review which aspects you did not check and set confidence score in the ARR form. If you know/guess the authors or have an academic COI (e.g., very close to your own work), contact the area chair for reassignment or recuse yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate parts you did not check
rubrics_metrics.description: If your expertise does not cover certain aspects of the submission (e.g., formal proofs), explicitly state in the review which major parts you did not check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps ACs interpret the review. For instance, note if you did not verify proofs or did not run experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Appropriateness (desk-reject consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the submission is appropriate for ARR and the scope of relevant CFPs; inappropriate scope may justify desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, consult ARR CFP and relevant conference CFPs. This check is usually quick and should not take more than ~30 minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Hallucinated references or citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Check carefully for hallucinated references, which are a serious concern for scientific reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot-check citations; flag references that do not exist or are misattributed. Hallucinated refs can be grounds for desk-rejection or ethics follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Anonymity violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should be properly anonymized; anonymity violations may be a desk-reject reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit references to authors' prior work, acknowledgements, or links to non-anonymous resources. If severe, notify AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Style guide or length violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Desk-reject if the paper does not follow style guides or exceeds page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page limits: 4 pages for short, 8 pages for long papers (excluding ethical considerations and limitations). Minor formatting issues may be fixable, but clear violations can justify desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Missing Limitations section
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the paper includes a Limitations section; missing it can be a significant issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If missing, flag as a problem. Requirement to include limitations is common in *CL venues and informs evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Inappropriate responses to the Responsible NLP checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the authors' responses to the Responsible NLP checklist are appropriate; egregious violations may qualify for desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for blanket or clearly incorrect answers (e.g., answering 'yes' when not applicable or providing no justification). Minor honest mistakes may be excused; goal is reasonable indication of where checklist answers are located.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer checklist — Possible ethics issues (flagging for ethics review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify potential ethics concerns (data collection, abuse risk, harms to minorities) and flag for a dedicated ethics review if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics issues are not automatic grounds for desk rejection but can lead to an extra ethics review. Provide justification when flagging; if lacking expertise, flag so the ACL ethics committee can evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for dual submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the submission is under review elsewhere or is a dual submission contrary to ARR rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you suspect dual submission, notify AC. ARR also performs checks, but reviewers should report seeing the same paper elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for extremely similar submissions / plagiarism / publication ethics violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for near-duplicate submissions, plagiarism, or other publication ethics violations and report them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify AC via official comment and coordinate incident report with publication ethics committee as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust expectations; read at least twice
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid critiquing during first read; read the paper at least twice (skim then in-depth) to avoid prototype/bias issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First, form a high-level impression (research question, approach) without looking at results; then perform detailed evaluation. This reduces hindsight and confirmation biases and the risk of penalizing unconventional paper types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skim-reading guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: On a skim read, identify research question and what was done; do NOT look at results yet to avoid hindsight bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What is the research question? Will the answer advance the field? Is the methodology and contribution type within the CFP scope?

rubrics_metrics.name: In-depth reading guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in-depth reading to evaluate technical soundness, validity of proofs, argumentation, novelty, and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How you evaluate depends on paper type; check supporting evidence, correctness of proofs, experimental methodology, and whether claims are supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should be readable by themselves; appendices may contain supplementary details but are not required reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are not obligated to examine appendices, but if the main text refers to appendix material critical for understanding, reviewers should check it. If material belongs in main text, suggest moving it there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific (I1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag issues specifically and in a way understandable to area chairs without reading the whole paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete statements: cite missing references by name, specify missing elements in descriptions, give line/section or exact examples. Avoid vague criticisms like 'not novel' without references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H1 — 'Results are not surprising' is not automatically a weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings that seem obvious in retrospect may still be valuable if not previously tested empirically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think results are unsurprising, check whether they were known or established; lack of prior testing can justify the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H2 — 'Results contradict expectations' beware confirmation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected results might reflect the data; reviewers should check for confirmation bias when reacting negatively to results that contradict beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-examine assumptions and evidence rather than dismissing surprising findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H3 — 'Not novel' requires references
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think a claimed novelty already exists, provide references (respect policy on concurrent work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If novelty concerns relate to reproduction/reimplementation/analysis contributions, treat them as valid contribution types per CFP when appropriately presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H4 — No precedent is not proof of lack of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly novel work tends to be harder to publish; novelty alone does not imply invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider novelty in context and avoid overly conservative rejections solely because something lacks precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H5 — Lacking SOTA is not necessarily a fault
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to surpass SOTA does not invalidate scientific contributions; other dimensions (efficiency, generalizability, interpretability, fairness) matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors do not claim SOTA, absence of SOTA results should not be treated as a reason to reject per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H6 — Negative results are valid contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers presenting negative results should not be discounted; such results can reduce hype and inform the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether negative results are supported by sound methodology and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H7 — Simpler methods can be preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity is not a weakness; simpler solutions can be less brittle and easier to deploy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize a method solely for being simple if it adequately solves the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H8 — Methodology preferences are not grounds for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dismiss work because it doesn't use your preferred methodology (e.g., deep learning); NLP includes many contribution types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize validity of diverse approaches: models, resources, surveys, analyses, position and theory papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H9 — Topic niche-ness is not necessarily a flaw
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrow topic can make a valuable main track paper if it contributes significantly to its subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate impact within the target community rather than dismissing niche topics outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H10 — Monolingual or non-English evaluation is valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing only on non-English languages or a single language does not automatically invalidate generalizability or significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monolingual work is valuable for practical and theoretical reasons; judge claims' scope appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H11 — Language errors vs content
rubrics_metrics.description: Language errors may be present, but clarity and scientific content should be prioritized over journalistic polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing is sufficiently clear, favor scientific content; suggest improvements for language rather than reject for minor errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H12 — Missing reference X policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Per ACL policy, missing references to highly relevant published work is a problem if that work was published (not just on arXiv) more than 3 months before the submission deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For resubmissions, comparisons are required only to relevant work published 3+ months before the original submission deadline. Otherwise suggest missing refs in suggestions section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H13 — Requests for extra experiments should be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Request extra experiments only if they are necessary to validate the claim; otherwise they belong in 'suggestions' not 'reasons to reject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for short papers, extra-experiment requests must be justified as required for claim validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H14 — Request comparisons to closed models only when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting comparisons to closed-source models (e.g., ChatGPT) is reasonable only if it directly bears on the claim, considering methodological problems like test contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blanket demands to compare to closed models; motivate such requests clearly if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H15 — 'Authors should have done X' is not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying 'I would have written this paper differently' is only a valid criticism if authors' choices prevent them from answering their research question or their framing is misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise treat such comments as suggestions rather than grounds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H16 — Limitations section is not automatically a weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations != weaknesses: acknowledging limitations is expected and should not automatically justify rejection unless they invalidate the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If limitations fully invalidate the work, motivate that claim explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic H17 — Citation count does not equal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Low citation counts do not imply invalidity; judging by citation count risks favoring well-known groups and narrowing research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work on its merits and contribution, not citation metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: M1 — LLM-only evaluation without validation
rubrics_metrics.description: If LLMs are used as automated evaluators, their reliability in this context must be sufficiently validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether authors validated LLM evaluators for the specific task; lack of validation is a methodological concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: M2 — Reproducibility issues
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be enough experimental detail to reproduce experiments (including hyperparameter selection); code/data availability should be clear or sufficiently motivated if not released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are not required to run code, but should assess whether enough detail is provided for reproducibility. Distinguish reproducibility (run same experiment) from replicability (reimplement). Reproducibility score should be justified in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: M3 — Undisclosed data quality issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets or resources with undisclosed quality issues are a serious problem and should be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are not obligated to examine raw data, but if you notice undisclosed problems, bring them up. Flag issues to authors/AC and possibly ethics reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: M4 — Unmotivated selection of models/benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should clearly motivate why their chosen models and benchmarks are appropriate and linked to the claimed contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different choices can be valid; critique only if the selected sample is inappropriate for the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: M5 — Incomplete assumptions or proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: All assumptions should be stated; formal statements must be supported by complete and correct proofs (which may be in appendices if referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proofs are incomplete or missing, flag as a serious issue. Note when proofs are delegated to appendices but not properly referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: T1 — Ethics issues with data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper involves human annotation or data collection, check Responsible NLP checklist items (ethics approval, compensation, consent) and consider flagging for ethics review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ethics aspects are satisfactorily addressed, you may still flag the paper for ethics review if unsure. Ethics reviewers will evaluate details and make recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: T2 — Unclear license / release terms for artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If authors contribute artifacts (datasets, trained models), their license and release terms should be clearly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are not legal adjudicators but should ensure authors specify release terms and clarify motivations; jurisdictional differences may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: R1 — Analysis issues (statistics, p-hacking, baseline tuning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for inappropriate/misleading statistics, p-hacking, selecting best runs without reporting variance, and poorly tuned baselines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request proper statistical reporting (error bars, confidence intervals, number of trials) and fair baseline tuning; call out potential cherry-picking.

rubrics_metrics.name: R2 — Inappropriate scope of the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the evaluated sample supports the population the authors claim about (e.g., claiming 'reasoning' from a few benchmarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sample does not represent the claimed population, request narrowing of claims or additional validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: R3 — Hypotheses/speculations presented as conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions must be based on evidence or clearly labeled as conjecture/speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag claims that overstep the evidence and ask authors to qualify speculative statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: R4 — Misleading or inappropriate framing and overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify framing that overstates what the experiments actually show (e.g., concluding 'understanding' without validating the construct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request reframing or additional validation to support broader claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: R5 — Inadequate statistical significance assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Main experimental results should include appropriate information about statistical significance, error bars, confidence intervals, and effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for details on how significance was computed and discussion of variability and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: G1 — Unclear research question or contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should clearly state the knowledge gap it addresses and what its contributions are in abstract and introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contributions or assumptions are unclear, ask authors to clarify and possibly reframe the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: G2 — Reliance on a bad precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: If methodology choices are motivated by precedent that is itself unsound, reviewers should explain and discuss this position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to evidence that a precedent is flawed and discuss alternatives; update review after discussion as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: G3 — Missing or misrepresented related work
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are expected to be aware of prior published work and to fairly represent others' contributions; missing or misrepresented related work is a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between missing preprints (<3 months) and missing published work (>3 months) per policy. For resubmissions, special rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: G4 — Key terms too vague and not defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Important terms must be defined or referenced; vague terminology undermines clarity and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to define key terms or point to standard definitions; suggest clarifications when terms are ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: G5 — Misleading or incorrect citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations should accurately reflect what is claimed about prior work; LLM-generated summaries can cause misattribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag misrepresentations, request correct citations and warnings about relying on automated summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use three scores: soundness, excitement, overall (I3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide three scores: soundness (must be justified by review text), excitement (subjective personal interest), and overall recommendation (composite reflecting soundness, excitement, novelty, impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify low soundness scores with explicit faults; excitement is orthogonal to soundness and may reflect taste. Overall score should reflect composite assessment; reproducibility scores should be justified as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: professional and neutral (I4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews must be professional, neutral, and constructive rather than sarcastic or insulting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reviews you would like to receive; avoid rude language and consider authors' possible vulnerabilities. Aim to help authors improve their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update assessment after authors' response (Task 4, I11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge authors' response and update your review if clarifications resolve concerns; add an explicit update note describing changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unconvinced, explain why briefly. Don’t just leave reviews unchanged; add 'Update: ...' statements indicating what changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in discussion with other reviewers and ACs
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in reviewer discussion before and after author response to catch mistakes, misunderstandings, or guideline violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs expect reviewers to respond and engage particularly after authors’ responses; prioritize concise, important clarifications for AC attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of social influence when reading other reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize how other reviewers' opinions may bias your judgment (e.g., convergence to mean or undue deference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether changes to your opinion are warranted by evidence or are social psychology effects. Strong disagreements may indicate novel/interesting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI policy for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must read the paper fully and write the content and arguments of their review themselves; using generative assistance to create the first draft (or meaningful meta-review arguments) is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed: responsible use such as paraphrasing to help non-native English speakers or tools that check proofs. Forbidden: uploading manuscripts or review text to non-privacy-preserving generative tools, or using such tools to produce first-draft reviews. Confidentiality of manuscripts and reviews extends to AI tool usage. Report suspect prompt injections in submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI guidance for authors (disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are obligated to disclose their use of generative AI in submissions (per ACL publication ethics); reviewers should be aware of this in Responsible NLP checklist (E1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you notice prompt injections or abuse of AI, raise with chairs — such submissions may be desk-rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary reviewer policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary reviewers may assist the main reviewer, but the main reviewer remains responsible for submitting the review and sustained engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a special field to acknowledge secondary reviewers (not visible to authors). Secondary reviewers can be credited in cycle-level records and request reviewer certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to handle resubmissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the submission is a resubmission (look for 'Previous URL' in metadata) and follow resubmission review guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the resubmissions section for special expectations (e.g., which comparisons are required based on original deadline). For resubmissions, check whether authors addressed prior critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and consequences for irresponsible reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: ARR collects author reports of poor reviews and ACs can nominate great or irresponsible reviewers; 'highly irresponsible' reviewers may be penalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported egregious cases (extremely terse, unprofessional, LLM-generated) can lead to desk-rejection of reviewer’s work for the cycle and temporary ineligibility to review/commit in subsequent cycles; ACs and program chairs can take action based on reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use review data irresponsibly; research data sharing opt-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymized review data can be shared for research only with consent of willing reviewers and authors; reviewers may opt in when setting availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ARR framework collects opt-in consents for data sharing; consider contributing to improve peer review research.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to contact area chair and use OpenReview
rubrics_metrics.description: Use OpenReview 'Official Comment' to contact ACs (select 'area chairs' in readers field) or use anonymized email link; follow OpenReview tutorials for common tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For AC-only communications use the Official Comment and select appropriate readers; email addresses on assignments pages may be anonymized but linked to homepages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to complete reviews on time — emergency and delay procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot complete an assignment due to personal emergency, use Emergency Declaration form; for short delays use Delay Notification form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forum forms rather than personal emails; emergency form triggers search for backup reviewers; misuse of delay mechanisms is discouraged and delayed reviews may affect 'great reviewer' recognition.
